title: Grids and matrices
objectives: Traverse, rotate and flood-fill a matrix without off-by-one errors.

screens.title: Round the edge
screens.prose: In `graphs-dp/l4-islands` you flood-filled a grid. Here you walk round one. Start at the top left and go clockwise along the edge until you are back next to the start.
screens.question: Tap every cell visited on the first lap.

hints.text: The first lap is the outer ring of the grid.
Every cell in row 0, row 2, column 0 or column 3 is on the ring.
Tap 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 11, 10, 9 and 5. Only 6 and 7 are inside.

feedback.correct: The first lap visits the 10 edge cells. 6 and 7 wait for the second lap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every cell on the outer ring and nothing inside it.

byKey.r2c2: 6 is not on the edge. It waits for the second lap.
byKey.r2c3: 7 is not on the edge. It waits for the second lap.

explain.text: The lap takes the top row, the right column, the bottom row backwards and the left column upwards. That is 10 cells. What is left, 6 and 7, is a smaller matrix with the same shape of problem.

screens.title: Step the spiral
screens.prose: Step through the whole spiral with the slider. Watch where each side of the lap starts and stops. The corners are where off-by-one errors hide.
screens.question: Which number does the spiral visit last?

widget.label: Last number
widget.accept: 7, the end of the second lap

hints.text: Slide to step 12.
After the first lap only 6 and 7 are left.
The second lap reads its top row, 6 then 7. So 7 is last.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to the last step and read the cell.

byKey.rowmajor: 12 is last in row order. The spiral passes 12 at step 6.
byKey.second: 6 starts the second lap. The lap goes on to 7.
byKey.lap: 5 ends the first lap. Two cells are still to come.

explain.text: Each lap is the edge of a smaller matrix: first 3 by 4, then 1 by 2. The second lap is a single row, with no right column, bottom row or left column of its own. That one-row case is the edge case of the next screen.

screens.title: One row, one column
screens.prose: Unchecked, a lap reads the top row, the right column, the bottom row backwards, then the left column up. On a 1 by 3 matrix that gives `[1, 2, 3, 2, 1]`. On a 3 by 1 it gives `[1, 2, 3, 2]`.
screens.question: Which two checks fix both shapes?

options.text: `if top < bottom:` before the bottom row, and `if left < right:` before the left column

options.why: Inside the `while` both are always true, so the 1 by 3 still reads its row twice.

options.text: Only `if top < bottom:` before the bottom row
options.why: That fixes the 1 by 3. The 3 by 1 still reads its middle cell again on the way up.

options.text: `if left < right:` before the bottom row, and `if top < bottom:` before the left column
options.why: You swapped them. On the 1 by 3, `left < right` is true, so the row is read again.

hints.text: When is the bottom row the same row as the top row?
On the 1 by 3, `top == bottom`.
Read the bottom row only when `top < bottom`, and the left column only when `left < right`.

feedback.correct: Each check stops a side that is the same cells as the side before it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what is equal when a side would be read twice.

byKey.b: You used `<=`. The `while` already guarantees it, so the check never stops anything.
byKey.c: You fixed rows only. A single column needs `left < right` before the left column.
byKey.d: You swapped the two checks. The bottom row repeats when `top == bottom`.

explain.text: When `top == bottom`, the bottom row is the top row read backwards. When `left == right`, the left column is the right column read upwards. The two checks skip exactly those repeats.

screens.title: Write the spiral
screens.prose: Keep four bounds: `top`, `bottom`, `left` and `right`. Read the four sides of the lap, with the two checks, then move every bound one step in. Stop when the bounds cross.
screens.question: Write `spiral_order(m)`: a rectangular matrix's entries in clockwise spiral order from the top left. Return `[]` for no rows.

tests.setup: m = [[r * 300 + c for c in range(300)] for r in range(300)]

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They cover square, wide and tall shapes, one cell, one row, one column, no rows and 300 by 300.

hints.text: What are the four bounds at the start?
`top, bottom, left, right = 0, len(m) - 1, 0, len(m[0]) - 1`.
Loop while `top <= bottom and left <= right`. Read the four sides: guard the bottom row with `top < bottom` and the left column with `left < right`. Then move all four bounds in.

feedback.correct: Four bounds, four sides, two checks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the 3 by 3. The spiral goes 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4, then 5.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is one row. Guard the bottom row with `top < bottom`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is one column. Guard the left column with `left < right`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has no rows. Return `[]` before reading `m[0]`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is 4 by 2. After one lap the bounds cross, so stop there.

explain.text: Each pass of the loop reads one lap and shrinks the bounds. The two checks handle a last lap of one row or one column. Every cell is read once, so the time is $O(rc)$.

screens.title: Where each entry goes
screens.prose: Turn a 5 by 5 matrix 90° clockwise. The top row becomes the right column, read downwards. Rows and columns here count from 0.

state.caption: The entry at row 0, column 1 holds 1

screens.question: Where does each entry go? Give its new row and column.

hints.text: The top row becomes the right column. Which column is that?
Row 0 lands in column 4. Its column number becomes the new row.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The old column becomes the new row, and the old row sets the new column.

byKey.r0c1: Check (0, 1). The old column, 1, is the new row.
byKey.r0c2: Check (0, 1). Row 0 becomes the right column, column 4.
byKey.r2c2: Check (4, 0). The bottom row becomes the left column, column 0.

explain.text: A clockwise turn sends $(r, c)$ to $(c, n - 1 - r)$. Transposing sends $(r, c)$ to $(c, r)$, and reversing each row then sends column $r$ to $n - 1 - r$. So the turn is a transpose followed by a reverse of every row.

canvas.caption: Old places in one colour, new places in the other

screens.title: Rotate in place
screens.prose: Transpose by swapping `m[r][c]` with `m[c][r]` above the diagonal only, then reverse each row. Change `m` itself: the tests keep their own reference to it.

state.caption: The entry at row 0, column 1 holds 1

screens.question: Write `rotate(m)`: turn an `n` by `n` matrix 90° clockwise in place, and return nothing.

tests.setup: m = [[r * 200 + c for c in range(200)] for r in range(200)]; rotate(m)

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each builds `m`, calls `rotate(m)` and then reads `m`, so a new list made inside the function is never seen.

hints.text: Which two steps make a clockwise turn?
Swap only above the diagonal: `c` runs from `r + 1`.
`for r in range(n): for c in range(r + 1, n): swap m[r][c] and m[c][r]`. Then `for row in m: row.reverse()`.

feedback.correct: Transpose, then reverse each row, both in place.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the 3 by 3. After `rotate(m)`, `m` must be `[[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 is the 2 by 2. If `m` is unchanged, check that you changed `m` and did not make a new list.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is 4 by 4. If you swap across the whole matrix, each pair swaps twice and nothing moves.

explain.text: Swapping only above the diagonal moves each pair once. Reversing each row then finishes the turn. Both steps change the caller's lists, so no new matrix is needed and extra memory is $O(1)$.

canvas.caption: The diagonal stays put in the transpose

screens.title: A new list with the old name
screens.prose:
A shorter attempt builds the turned matrix in one line.

```python
def rotate(m):
    m = [list(row) for row in zip(*m[::-1])]
```

The console shows a call.
screens.question: Why is the caller's `m` unchanged?

options.text: It points its local name `m` at a new list
`zip` gives tuples, which cannot be changed
options.why: The tuples became lists with `list(row)`. Nothing at all changed in the caller's list.

options.text: The formula turns the wrong way
options.why: A wrong turn would still change `m`. Here it did not change at all.

options.text: Python copies a list when it is passed to a function
options.why: Python passes a reference to the same list. Changing `m[0]` inside would show outside.

hints.text: What does `m = ...` do inside a function?
It rebinds a local name. The caller still holds the old list.
Assigning to the name changes what the name points at, not the list. Write `m[:] = ...` to fill the caller's list.

feedback.correct: Rebinding the name leaves the caller's list as it was.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what object the caller's `m` refers to after the call.

byKey.b: You blamed the tuples. `list(row)` turned them into lists, and the caller still saw nothing.
byKey.c: You blamed the direction. A wrong turn would still change `m`.
byKey.d: You assumed a copy. Python passes the same list, so a change through it would show.

explain.text: `m = [...]` makes the local name point at a new list and drops it on return. The caller's list was never changed. `m[:] = [...]` replaces the contents of the caller's list, or rotate in place as before.

canvas.caption: The caller still holds the old list

screens.title: Safe from the border
screens.prose: On this board, every group of `O` cells that does not touch the border is captured and becomes `X`. Groups join up, down, left and right, not diagonally.
screens.question: Tap every `O` that cannot be captured.

hints.text: Which `O` cells sit on the border?
Two `O`s touch the border: the last cell of the third row and the bottom of the second column.
Tap the border `O`s and every `O` joined to them: the right-hand group of three and the left column pair.

feedback.correct: Five cells join the border: three on the right, two on the left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the `O`s on the border and follow their neighbours.

byKey.r2c2: This cell's group of three touches no border cell, so it is captured.
byKey.r2c3: This cell's group of three touches no border cell, so it is captured.
byKey.r3c3: This cell joins the group of three above it, which touches no border cell. It is captured.

explain.text: Start from the `O`s on the border and spread to `O` neighbours. Everything reached is safe; every other `O` is captured. Searching from the border is easier than testing each inner group.

screens.title: Capture the regions
screens.prose: Seed a stack with every border `O`, spread through `O` neighbours, and mark what you reach as safe. Then build new rows. Use a stack, not recursion: the last test is 400 by 400.

state.caption: Safe cells shaded; the other `O`s become `X`

screens.question: Write `capture_regions(board)`: every `O` group that does not touch the border becomes `X`. Return a new list of strings.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They include one cell, a ring of `O` round an `X` and a 400 by 400 board.

hints.text: Which cells do you know are safe without searching?
Every `O` on the border is safe.
Push every border `O`. Pop a cell, add it to `safe`, and push its `O` neighbours not yet safe. Then rebuild each row: `O` stays only if it is in `safe`.

feedback.correct: Seeded from the border, the search touches each cell at most a few times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has an inner group of three and a border `O`. Only the border one survives.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is one `O` inside a ring of `X`. It is captured.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has a middle `O` that touches others only diagonally. It is captured.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 is 400 by 400. A recursive search from each cell is too deep or too slow; use one stack seeded from the border.

explain.text: The border seeds hold every cell that can be safe, so one search finds them all. Each cell is pushed at most four times, so the time is $O(rc)$. A stack avoids Python's recursion limit on large boards.

screens.title: The four bounds
screens.prose:
All three problems avoid off-by-one errors the same way: name the edges, then move them.

```python
top, bottom, left, right = 0, R - 1, 0, C - 1
while top <= bottom and left <= right:
    ...                  # read one lap
    top += 1; bottom -= 1; left += 1; right -= 1
```
screens.question: Put one lap of the spiral in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Read the top row from `left` to `right`
Read the right column from `top + 1` to `bottom`
If `top < bottom`, read the bottom row from `right - 1` back to `left`
If `left < right`, read the left column from `bottom - 1` back to `top + 1`
Move all four bounds one step in
Read the right column from `top` to `bottom`
lines.why: The top row already read the top-right corner, so it would appear twice.

hints.text: Go clockwise from the top left.
Each side starts one cell after the corner the previous side ended on.
Loop, top row, right column from `top + 1`, guarded bottom row, guarded left column, shrink. Leave out the right column from `top`.

feedback.correct: Four sides, each starting past the last corner, then the bounds move in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the lap clockwise from the top left.

byKey.d1: You started the right column at `top`. The top row already took that corner.
byKey.left-out: Every line but one belongs. Only the right column from `top` is wrong.

explain.text: Each side starts one past the corner the previous side ended on, so no corner is read twice. The two checks drop a side that would repeat the previous one. Moving all four bounds together keeps the next lap a rectangle.

screens.title: The edge of a heat map
screens.prose: A risk screen shows a book's depth as a grid: price levels down the side, minutes across. It prints the outer ring clockwise from the top left, to flag stale edges.

state.caption: Resting size, in lots, at each price and minute

screens.question: Which sequence does it print?

options.why: You read row by row. The ring follows the edge: down the right column after the top row.
You went anticlockwise, down the left column first.
You read the bottom row left to right. Clockwise, it runs right to left: 11, 12, 1, 10.

hints.text: Top row first, then which side?
After 7 the ring goes down the right column: 3, then 11.
Top row 5, 8, 2, 7; right column 3, 11; bottom row backwards 12, 1, 10; left column up 4.

feedback.correct: Top, right, bottom backwards, left upwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the edge clockwise from the top left.

byKey.b: You printed in row order. That is not a ring.
byKey.c: You went down first. Clockwise from the top left goes right first.
byKey.d: You read the bottom row the wrong way. Clockwise means right to left along the bottom.

explain.text: The ring is the first lap of the spiral: 10 of the 12 cells. The two inner cells, 9 and 6, are not printed. The same four-bounds code prints any ring by stopping after one lap.

screens.title: Where a big spiral ends
screens.prose: A scenario grid of 300 by 300 P&Ls is stored row by row. Row $r$, column $c$ holds $300r + c$. A report walks it in spiral order. Each lap removes one ring.

state.caption: The 3 by 4 ends one row below and one column left of the middle

screens.question: What is the last value the spiral visits?

hints.text: After 150 laps, how many rows and columns are left?
Each lap removes 2 rows and 2 columns. The 149th lap leaves rows 149 to 150 and columns 149 to 150.
That 2 by 2 is read 44,849, 44,850, 45,150, then 45,149. So the last is row 150, column 149: $300 \times 150 + 149$.

feedback.correct: The last lap is a 2 by 2, which ends at its bottom left: 45,149.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last ring, then where its lap ends.

byKey.centre: 45,150 is the bottom right of the last 2 by 2. The lap goes on to the bottom left.
byKey.swap: 44,850 is row 149, column 150. The lap ends one row lower, at row 150, column 149.
byKey.last: 89,999 is last in row order. The spiral ends near the middle.

explain.text: After 149 laps a 2 by 2 is left, rows and columns 149 and 150. Its lap reads top left, top right, bottom right, then bottom left. The bottom left holds $300 \times 150 + 149 = 45{,}149$.

ideas: A spiral keeps four bounds and shrinks them after each lap. `top < bottom` and `left < right` stop a last row or column being read twice.
A clockwise turn sends $(r, c)$ to $(c, n - 1 - r)$: transpose above the diagonal, then reverse each row, all in place.
Flood fill from the cells you know are safe, here the border, with a stack rather than recursion.
summary.trap: `m = [...]` inside the function rebinds the name, so the caller's matrix is unchanged. Change the list itself.

quiz.question: A 5 by 6 matrix (5 rows) has finished its first lap. What are `top, bottom, left, right` now?

options.why: You moved only `top` and `left`. All four bounds move in after a lap.
Those are the starting bounds. One lap moves each in by one.
You moved `right` but not `bottom`. Every bound moves in.

feedback.correct: Every bound moves one step in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from `0, 4, 0, 5` and move each bound in.

explain.text: The bounds start at `0, 4, 0, 5`. After a lap `top` and `left` go up by one, `bottom` and `right` down by one: `1, 3, 1, 4`.

quiz.question: Transpose `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`, then reverse each row. Which way has it turned?

options.why: That is a transpose followed by reversing the order of the rows.
A half turn reverses the rows and each row. Transpose then row reverse is a quarter turn.
You reversed each row but skipped the transpose.

feedback.correct: Transpose gives `[[1, 3], [2, 4]]`; reversing each row gives `[[3, 1], [4, 2]]`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do the two steps on paper.

explain.text: The transpose is `[[1, 3], [2, 4]]`. Reversing each row gives `[[3, 1], [4, 2]]`, the top row turned into the right column. That is clockwise.

quiz.question: How many `O` cells does `capture_regions` turn into `X`?

widget.label: Captured
widget.accept: 2: the two `O`s in the second row

feedback.correct: The two `O`s in row 1 are enclosed. The bottom row's `O`s touch the border.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Any `O` on the border, or joined to one, survives.

byKey.all: You captured every `O`. The three in the bottom row sit on the border.
byKey.inner: You captured the bottom pair. Cells on the bottom row touch the border.

explain.text: The bottom row is a border, so its three `O`s are safe. The two `O`s in row 1 are surrounded by `X`. So 2 are captured.

quiz.question: Rotating an `n` by `n` matrix by building a new one uses how much extra memory? Compare it with the in-place method.

options.why: The new matrix holds all $n^2$ entries, not one row.
In place swaps two entries at a time and keeps only a few variables.
You swapped them. The copy is the one that needs a second matrix.

feedback.correct: A copy holds $n^2$ entries; in place needs a few variables.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does each method keep besides `m`?

explain.text: Building a new matrix stores $n^2$ more entries. Transposing and reversing in place keeps only the loop indices. Both take $O(n^2)$ time.
